name: Colin Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for doing this, Colin. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything here is confidential. Can you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on an underground and new-connections crew in the south suburbs, where they're throwing up housing estates as fast as they can. Most days it's hooking up new houses, pulling cable through ducts, putting in pad-mount transformers, and lately a lot of EV chargers and heat pumps that need bigger supply. I start at seven at the depot on Larch Road with Ana, my crew lead, and we usually knock out three or four jobs.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy about it, and what drains you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love that I'm basically wiring up the future, every new solar roof and charger goes through someone like me. I use an AI assistant every day to read the long spec sheets and to quiz me for my cable jointer certificate in the evenings. What drains me is the developers, who always want the power on yesterday and never have the trench ready when we arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fair enough, it's a better search engine and that's it. I'd probably post that the real revolution is the electrification stuff I'm already doing, heat pumps and chargers and batteries. At work I'd say AI just saved me reading a hundred pages of specs, and that's nice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's fine, maybe even good. I've got about nine months saved plus some index funds, and in the south suburbs there's more work than crews. Sam, my boyfriend, tests software for an insurance company, and even a small change there would mean some of his routine checking gets automated, but he'd shrug it off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing and finish the cable jointer certificate by next summer. I'd keep using the AI assistant for specs and studying, and maybe try a better one if it comes out. Nothing big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly disappointed, honestly, because I like new toys.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Sam would shrug off small changes. Would you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, if it's small. Sam's team already uses scripts that do half the checking, and he just moved on to the harder stuff. If it stays at that level, we're both fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the thing that would actually change your life in this picture, if not AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting the jointer ticket will change my life more than AI, because jointers get called out for the big underground faults. They make more too, and I find that fault work really satisfying. That's my next five years.

say: I'd say AI is a **better search engine** and nothing more.
I'd post that the real revolution is **electrification**: heat pumps, chargers and batteries.
think: My work and money feel **secure**, with **nine months saved** and plenty of crews needed.
Sam's **software testing** job would see small changes he can shrug off.
do: Finish the **cable jointer** certificate by next summer.
Keep using the **AI assistant** for specs and evening study.
feel: **Calm**, and slightly **disappointed** because he likes new tools.

fieldNote: He sees **electrification**, not AI, as the big change in his own work.

He already tracks how changes hit **Sam's job**, the more exposed income at home.

steps.text: Finish the cable jointer certificate by next summer
Keep using the AI assistant to read spec sheets

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud: this is great for trades and rough for desk jobs, and we should be honest about that. Online I'd push for the government to pay for retraining people coming out of offices into electrical work, because we're short of hands. At work I'd say the design office is going to get very small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be thinking about Sam every day. Checking and coding are right there on the list, and my boyfriend Sam's team at the insurer is twelve people who mostly check things. My own job barely moves, the AI would do the design drawings and the permits faster, which honestly would help us, but Sam's job could realistically shrink in the next couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Sam in the first month and look at what he could move into, maybe the AI testing side, maybe something else. I'd put more aside each month so we have a bigger cushion if his pay drops, and I'd keep pushing on my jointer certificate. I'd also learn whatever AI design tool the office starts using, so I can check their drawings before we dig.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more for us as a household than for me. I'd feel useful, too, because I'm the safe one for once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Sam's the exposed one. What's the conversation at home like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd play it down, he always does. I'd probably make him a spreadsheet of what we spend and show him we're fine on my wage alone, which we are. Then I'd nudge him to take a course while his employer still pays for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the design office would get small. Does that affect your crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, in a good way at first. Right now we wait weeks for a design on a new estate, and if AI does that in a day, we'd have more work, not less. The worry is whether the AI drawing is right, because a wrong duct route means we dig twice.

Online I'd push for government-paid **retraining** of office workers into electrical work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for a real safety net, something like a basic income paid for by the companies that own the AI. I'd say it at the union and I'd say it loudly online. At work I'd tell people the trades have three years, so use them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, Sam's job is gone by 2028, I'm pretty sure of that. Mine has maybe until 2031, when I'm thirty-two, and underground work in a muddy trench is messy, so maybe a bit longer. But I'd expect the new-connection work, which is very repetitive, to be one of the first things robots do, and that's exactly my crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd double my savings and stop buying anything big. I'd look for a course in robotics maintenance, because when robots are pulling cable, somebody has to fix them, and I'd rather that be me. I'd push the union hard to get members trained on the robots before the company brings in outside technicians, and I'd campaign for the basic income thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake doing the maths on two incomes going to one and then maybe none.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're the adaptive one. Doesn't part of you find this exciting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, honestly, part of me does. If I'm the guy who knows how the cable-pulling robot works, that's a good job for a while. But it's hard to be excited when the person you live with just lost his job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ana, your crew lead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to get on the robot training list the day it opens. Ana's forty-five and brilliant, but she hates screens. If she waits, she'll be the one they let go.

At work I'd tell people the trades have **three years**, so use them.
think: Sam's job is **gone by 2028**, I'm pretty sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years to get this right, so let's build the training now, not after. I'd be the person at the union meeting with a slide about which jobs go when. Online I'd say the same, with a bit less shouting than the fast version.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years changes a lot for Sam. He'd have time to move, maybe into something with people, maybe even into trades with me. For me, robots by 2034 means I'm thirty-five, and I'd want to already be a jointer and halfway into robot maintenance by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the jointer ticket in the first year and then start the robotics course part-time. Sam and I would put a chunk of our savings into a small rental flat, so we have income that doesn't come from either of our jobs. I'd get on the union's technology committee and push for a training fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a busy, organised way. I'd have a plan on the fridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A rental flat is a big step. Why that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if both our jobs get eaten, rent from a flat still comes in. We've got enough for a deposit on a small one-bedroom near the train line. It's not exciting, it's just a floor under us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Sam feel about moving into trades?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd laugh at first, he's never held a drill. But he's careful and patient, which is exactly what a good jointer needs. I'd take him to the depot on an open day and let Ana sell it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where nobody has an excuse. Ten years is two apprenticeships long, and nobody has an excuse in this version. I'd say that at work and online, and I'd keep saying the companies should pay for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm fairly comfortable here. Sam has until 2036 and I have until about 2039, when I'm forty, and I'll be a jointer with a robotics ticket long before then. The thing that still bugs me is the people around me who won't move, because ten years can feel like forever until it doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and finish the jointer certificate, and start playing with every robotics and AI tool I can get my hands on, the way I do now. In year two or three I'd do the robotics course. We'd probably buy the rental flat a bit later, once we'd saved more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly for other people. For myself I'd feel like I can see the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who are the people who won't move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half my depot, honestly. The guys who say robots will never get in a trench. Ten years is plenty of time to prove them wrong, and nobody will be listening when it does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything in your own life you'd do differently because of this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I'd think harder about where we buy a house. Somewhere with good trains and a mix of jobs, not a town that lives off one depot. That's about it.

I'd keep saying **companies** should pay for the change.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without a doubt, because Sam and I would get hit one after the other with no time to plan. What would help is training on the robots for the people already doing the work, paid for by the companies, and some kind of basic income so a lost job isn't a lost life.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the good side. If robots can build the grid, we could electrify everything much faster, and that matters for the climate. I'd just want the people who built the old grid to share in it.

headlineQuote: If I'm the guy who knows how the cable-pulling robot works, that's a good job for a while.
portrait: Colin is a **27-year-old** underground lineworker hooking up new estates, chargers and heat pumps.
He lives with Sam, a **software tester**, and studies for a **jointer ticket** with daily AI help.
He's calm in AI Plateau but **anxious** in Steady Disruption because Sam's job is exposed.
The fast AGI version **alarms** him; slower ones turn into training, a rental flat and union work.
He's a progressive optimist who wants **workers to share** the gains of a robot-built grid.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with Sam and then himself hit back to back and no time to plan.
whatWouldHelp: Company-paid **robot training** for current workers and a **basic income** as a safety net.
